cards.q: What is antenatal care (ANC) and what is an antenatal visit?
cards.a:
• **ANC** = care by a **skilled health-care professional** addressing both the **medical and psychological** needs of pregnant women
• Goal: best health for **mother and baby** throughout pregnancy
• **Antenatal visit** = a **series of scheduled check-ups** attended throughout pregnancy
cards.m: ANC looks after TWO patients and TWO needs (body + mind).

cards.q: List the four core objectives of the antenatal visit (MOH Perinatal Care Manual).
cards.a:
• **Screen** for risk factors
• Identify and manage women with **bad obstetric history** and **medical complications**
• Encourage **spouse/partner/family involvement** during visits
• Identify the mother's **needs and wants** and give **emotional support**
cards.m: S-B-F-E: Screen, Bad history, Family, Emotions.

cards.q: What is the routine antenatal visit frequency for a pregnant woman in Malaysia (as taught on the slides)?
cards.a:
• **Booking visit** as early as possible
• **Monthly** until **28 weeks**
• **Every 2 weeks** from **28 to 36 weeks**
• **Weekly** from **36 weeks until delivery**
• High-risk pregnancies need **more frequent** visits
cards.m: 4-2-1: every 4 weeks, then every 2, then every 1 (break-points 28 and 36).

cards.q: What are the three types of antenatal visit and the benefits of the virtual option?
cards.a:
• **Physical** visit, **virtual** visit, **home** visit
• High-risk: more frequent **physical** visits
• Low-risk: **virtual consultation** if eligible
• Virtual benefits: **fewer clinic visits**, better **access and convenience**, mother attends **comfortably from home**

cards.q: When should the booking visit be done, and what if the mother comes late?
cards.a:
• **As early as possible**, preferably **before 12 weeks**
• A **first visit done later is still the booking visit**
• Why early: accurate **dating scan**, early **infection/thalassaemia screening**, early **supplements** and risk coding
cards.m: Book before the baby is 12 weeks old in the womb.

cards.q: When are the first and second Routine Medical Examinations (RME) done in antenatal care?
cards.a:
• **First RME**: by a **doctor** during or **within 2 weeks after the booking visit**
• **Second RME**: by a **Medical Officer** between **32 and 36 weeks**
• Purpose: doctor-level review of risk, examination and plan for delivery
cards.m: RME-1 near booking; RME-2 near the finish line (32-36 w).

cards.q: What history must be recorded at the booking visit?
cards.a:
• **Menstrual** history (LMP for dating)
• **Medical** and **past surgical** history
• **Past obstetric** history
• **Family** history
• **Socio-economic** background
cards.m: MMSOFS: Menstrual, Medical, Surgical, Obstetric, Family, Social.

cards.q: What physical examination and imaging are done at the booking visit?
cards.a:
• **BMI**, **blood pressure**, **heart rate**
• General assessment and **systemic** examination
• **Abdominal** and **vaginal** examination (when indicated)
• **Ultrasound** to confirm **viability and dating**

cards.q: What laboratory investigations are done at booking?
cards.a:
• **Urinalysis**: protein, sugar (**UFEME** if indicated)
• **Blood**: **Hb**, **platelets**, **blood group and Rhesus**
• **Infection screen for all**: **syphilis**, **HIV**, **hepatitis B**
• **If indicated**: **thalassaemia**, **malaria**, **TB**
cards.m: Booking bloods = ABC + SHH: Anaemia, Blood group, Count (platelet) + Syphilis, HIV, Hep B.

cards.q: Why are syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B screened in every pregnant woman?
cards.a:
• All three can be **transmitted vertically** and are **treatable/preventable**
• Syphilis: **benzathine penicillin** prevents congenital syphilis
• HIV: **antiretroviral therapy** + safe delivery/feeding plan reduces transmission to <2%
• Hep B: baby gets **hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG at birth**
cards.m: Screen what you can stop.

cards.q: What management is started at the booking visit?
cards.a:
• **Folic acid** and **iron** supplements
• **Nutritional advice**
• **Health education**
• **Information on antenatal screening** tests

cards.q: What is checked at every subsequent antenatal physical visit?
cards.a:
• **Hb** level **monthly**
• **Weight** and **BP**
• **Urine** for **protein and glucose**
• **Symphysio-fundal height** (SFH)
• Ask about relevant **symptoms**
• **Lie, presentation and head engagement**, especially **after 36 weeks**
cards.m: Every visit: Blood (Hb), BP, Bladder (urine), Belly (SFH), Baby (lie).

cards.q: How is symphysio-fundal height (SFH) interpreted and when does a discrepancy need action?
cards.a:
• From **24 weeks**, SFH in cm ≈ **gestational age in weeks (± 2 cm)**
• SFH **smaller than dates** by >2-3 cm: think **fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, wrong dates**
• SFH **larger than dates**: **macrosomia (GDM), polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy**
• Next step: **ultrasound** for growth and liquor
cards.m: Centimetres = weeks.

cards.q: Which pregnant women need an OGTT for gestational diabetes (Malaysian CPG risk factors)?
cards.a:
• **BMI >27 kg/m²**
• **Previous GDM**
• **First-degree relative** with diabetes
• Previous baby **≥4 kg** or bad obstetric history (unexplained stillbirth)
• **Glycosuria ≥2+** on two occasions
• **Age ≥25 years**; current **polyhydramnios** or hypertension
• Test at **booking**; if normal **repeat at 24-28 weeks**
cards.m: Malaysia screens almost everyone: age ≥25 alone qualifies.

cards.q: Who is eligible for an antenatal virtual consultation?
cards.a:
• An **option, not compulsory**
• Proposed **only for white-tagged mothers**
• **Green-coded** mothers must first be **assessed by an MO** for suitability
• **Not eligible**: mothers with **social issues** (e.g. poor social support) or **poor compliance / missed appointments**
cards.m: Virtual is a privilege for the lowest risk and the reliable.

cards.q: At what gestations are the first and second antenatal virtual consultations scheduled?
cards.a:
• **First** virtual consultation: **24-26 weeks**
• **Second** virtual consultation: **32-34 weeks**
• Physical visits remain for booking, RME and investigations
cards.m: Virtual visits sit at the mid-points: 25 and 33 weeks.

cards.q: Which green-coding factors related to parity and blood group still allow virtual consultation?
cards.a:
• **Primigravida / pseudoprimigravida** (only if **<36 years**)
• **Grand multipara ≥5**
• **Rhesus negative**
• **Age 35/36-39** (multigravida only)
• Note: slides p10 and p11 give the age band as 36-39 and 35-39 respectively
cards.m: Green = mild risk you can still watch remotely.

cards.q: Which past obstetric history factors give a green code (still eligible for virtual review)?
cards.a:
• **Recurrent miscarriage (≥3 consecutive)**
• Previous baby **>4 kg**
• Previous **3rd/4th-degree perineal tear**
• Previous **retained placenta** or **PPH**
• Previous **instrumental delivery**
• Note: slide p11 says '≥3 consecutive marriages' - correct term is **miscarriages**
cards.m: Big baby, Bad tear, Bleed, Bits retained, Barrel (forceps/vacuum).

cards.q: Which body-size, dating and gynaecological factors give a green code?
cards.a:
• **Booking weight <45 kg** (risk of growth restriction)
• **Height <145 cm** (risk of **cephalopelvic disproportion**)
• **Unsure of dates**
• Previous **gynaecological surgery** (e.g. fibroid, cyst)
• **Birth spacing <2 years or >5 years**
cards.m: 45 kg and 145 cm - two 45s to remember.

cards.q: What does each colour in the MOH antenatal colour coding system mean for level of care?
cards.a:
• **Red**: **immediate referral to hospital**; then shared care O&G / FMS
• **Yellow**: **referral for management** by hospital O&G specialist / FMS; later shared care with MO & nurses
• **Green**: managed at **health clinic by MO & nurses**
• **White**: care by **health/community nurses** at KK and Klinik Desa
cards.m: Traffic light plus a blank page: Red stop-go now, Yellow get a specialist, Green MO, White nurse.

cards.q: When is a mother given a white code?
cards.a:
• When she has **no risk factors** listed under **red, yellow or green**
• Care by **health nurses / community nurses** at the **health clinic and rural clinic (Klinik Desa)**
• Re-code at every visit: risk can appear later
cards.m: White = clean sheet.

cards.q: Give classic examples of antenatal conditions that are red-coded (immediate hospital referral).
cards.a:
• **Imminent eclampsia**: severe headache, blurred vision, epigastric pain with high BP
• **Fits** (eclampsia)
• **BP ≥160/110 mmHg**
• **Antepartum haemorrhage**
• **Breathlessness / chest pain** (e.g. cardiac disease, PE)
• **Preterm labour** or **leaking liquor**
cards.m: Red = Fits, Bleeds, Blows (BP), Breathless, Born early.

cards.q: Red versus yellow antenatal code: what is the practical difference?
cards.a:
• **Red**: send **now** - **immediate referral** (stabilise, escort/ambulance) to hospital
• **Yellow**: **planned referral** to hospital O&G specialist / FMS for a management plan, then **shared care** with MO and nurses
• Both leave the woman under specialist decision-making
cards.m: Red = ambulance today; Yellow = appointment letter.

cards.q: Why are maternal weight, BP and urine protein checked at every antenatal visit?
cards.a:
• **BP + proteinuria**: early detection of **pre-eclampsia** (after 20 weeks)
• **Urine glucose**: clue to **GDM**
• **Weight**: poor gain suggests **under-nutrition/growth restriction**; excess gain suggests **GDM, oedema, polyhydramnios**
• Hb: detects **anaemia** - the commonest antenatal problem in KK

cards.q: Which pregnant women need an antenatal home visit?
cards.a:
• **New cases**
• **Defaulters** of follow-up
• **High-risk** mothers
cards.m: N-D-H: New, Defaulter, High-risk.

cards.q: How many antenatal home visits are needed?
cards.a:
• **Normal antenatal mother**: **one** home visit is adequate
• **High-risk mothers**: **more frequent** visits depending on **severity of risk**
• **Defaulters** also need more frequent visits

cards.q: What should be done during an antenatal home visit?
cards.a:
• Assess **general health and vital signs**
• Assess **fetal growth and wellbeing**
• Review **compliance with supplements** (iron, folic acid)
• Identify **danger signs**
• Assess **hygiene and living conditions**
• Educate **family** on support and danger signs
• Counsel on **diet and birth preparedness**
cards.m: Mum, Baby, Pills, Danger, Home, Family, Plan.

cards.q: What are the common challenges of antenatal home visits?
cards.a:
• **Wrong phone number** or **wrong address**
• **Mother not at home**
• **Limited time**
• **Cannot enter the house**
• Tip: confirm address and appointment by phone, use landmarks, visit with a colleague

cards.q: What is the protocol for entering and conducting an antenatal home visit?
cards.a:
• **Enter only after obtaining permission**
• **Respect** the mother and family
• **Communicate well** to build **rapport**
• **Explain the objectives** of the visit clearly
• **Avoid unfavourable comments or judgement** about the patient and family
cards.m: Permission, Respect, Rapport, Reason - then examine.

cards.q: In what order should the health worker proceed once inside the home?
cards.a:
• **Develop rapport first**
• Then take **history and physical examination**
• First ascertain **progress of pregnancy** and **wellbeing of the mother**
• **Update the antenatal book** (Buku Rekod Kesihatan Ibu)

cards.q: A mother prefers home delivery. What should the health worker do at the antenatal home visit?
cards.a:
• If she **meets all criteria** for home delivery: **check the intended birth site** and advise on **necessary preparation**
• If she **needs hospital or an Alternative Birthing Centre (ABC)**: advise on the **facility and its locality**
• Educate on hygiene and sanitation

cards.q: What should be done if a home visit finds that basic facilities are lacking?
cards.a:
• **Refer to the relevant unit**
• Example: **no toilet** → **environmental sanitation unit**
• Educate mother and family on **personal hygiene and sanitation**

cards.q: What is the tetanus toxoid (TT) schedule for a primigravida?
cards.a:
• **First dose at quickening**
• **Second dose 4 weeks later**
• Purpose: prevent **maternal and neonatal tetanus** via transplacental antibody
cards.m: Primi = two shots, 4 weeks apart, starting when baby first kicks.

cards.q: What is the tetanus toxoid schedule for a multigravida?
cards.a:
• **A single dose**
• Given **between quickening and before 37 weeks** of gestation
cards.m: Multi = one booster.

cards.q: When does quickening occur and why does it matter for maternal vaccination?
cards.a:
• First perceived fetal movements: about **18-20 weeks in a primigravida**, **16-18 weeks in a multigravida**
• TT is timed from quickening: after organogenesis, and early enough for antibodies to cross the placenta before birth

cards.q: When is Tdap recommended in pregnancy and why?
cards.a:
• **Recommended between 28-36 weeks** (listed as optional on the slide)
• Protects the **newborn from pertussis**
• Why: maternal **IgG crosses the placenta** and covers the baby until infant DTaP starts at 2 months
• Give in **every pregnancy**
cards.m: Tdap = Tiny-baby defence against pertussis.

cards.q: What is recommended about influenza and COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Influenza**: recommended for **all pregnant mothers**, especially **>20 weeks**; use **inactivated** vaccine
• Why: pregnancy raises risk of **severe influenza**; antibodies also protect infants <6 months
• **COVID-19**: **offer to all unvaccinated** mothers and explain its importance

cards.q: Which vaccines are given in pregnancy for specific populations?
cards.a:
• **Asplenia**: **Hib, meningococcal and pneumococcal** (2 doses, **5-yearly booster**)
• **Travel to endemic areas**: **typhoid, yellow fever, meningococcal**
• **Hepatitis A**: **liver disease, sewage workers, IV drug users, haemophilia**

cards.q: Which vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Live vaccines**: **MMR/rubella, varicella, BCG, oral typhoid, live intranasal influenza**
• **Yellow fever** (live): only if travel to a high-risk area is **unavoidable**
• Inactivated vaccines (TT, Tdap, influenza, hepatitis B) are safe
• Note: slide p16 lists yellow fever for travellers without this caveat
cards.m: Live vaccines wait until the baby is out.

cards.q: A pregnant woman is found to be rubella non-immune. What is the plan?
cards.a:
• **Do not give MMR in pregnancy** (live vaccine)
• Avoid contact with rash illnesses
• Give **MMR immediately postpartum** (safe while breastfeeding)
• Inadvertent MMR in pregnancy is **not an indication for termination**

cards.q: Define the postpartum period (puerperium) and its duration.
cards.a:
• From the **end of labour** until the **reproductive organs return to their non-pregnant state**
• Lasts **42 days (6 weeks)**
cards.m: 42 days = 6 weeks: the puerperium ends at the 6-week check.

cards.q: What are the eight aims of postnatal care?
cards.a:
• **Support** mother and family through the transition
• **Prevent, detect and treat complications**, incl. **vertical transmission**
• **Refer** for specialist care when necessary
• Counsel on **baby care and immunisation**
• Support **breastfeeding**
• Counsel on **maternal nutrition and exercise**
• **Contraception** and resumption of **sexual activity**; **emotional/psychological support**

cards.q: What is a postnatal 'contact'?
cards.a:
• An **active encounter** between the woman and a health-care provider
• Through **home visits, clinic visits, phone calls or mobile phone-based contacts**
• Counts whether in person or remote

cards.q: How often should postnatal contacts occur in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Uncomplicated** pregnancy and delivery: **at least 5 contacts**
• **High-risk** mothers and babies: **more frequent**
• Birth at an **Alternative Birthing Centre (ABC)** or **at home**: **home visit within 24 hours** of delivery

cards.q: What is the WHO minimum postnatal contact schedule?
cards.a:
• **At least 4** postnatal contacts
• First: facility birth - **at least 24 hours in facility**; home birth - **as early as possible within 24 hours**
• Then **day 3**, **days 7-14** and **6 weeks** after birth

cards.q: What is the Malaysian minimum postnatal visit schedule and how does it differ from WHO?
cards.a:
• Malaysia: minimum **5 home visits + 1 clinic visit**
• Adds **day 5** and **day 14-16** home visits to the WHO contacts (expert committee consensus)
• Day 5: also when **suitability for virtual follow-up** is assessed
cards.m: Malaysia = WHO + 5 + 15.

cards.q: State the rules for postnatal high-risk stratification.
cards.a:
• Done **before discharge**
• Any **postnatal readmission** is **re-triaged** before discharge
• Also applies **after miscarriage or termination of pregnancy**
• List is **not exhaustive**: any mother or newborn needing higher care is **tagged high-risk**

cards.q: What are the three components of postnatal care delivery?
cards.a:
• **Home visits**
• **Clinic visits**
• **Virtual consultation** (for eligible low-risk mothers)

cards.q: What should be assessed in the mother at a postnatal home visit?
cards.a:
• **General wellbeing**, **vital signs**
• **Lochia**, **urinary and bowel** function
• **Wound healing**, **perineal pain and hygiene**
• **Breastfeeding** progress, **breast pain**
• **Calf pain** (DVT)
• **Emotional wellbeing**, family and social support; **postnatal depression**
• Nutrition, hygiene and **contraception**
cards.m: BUBBLE-HE: Breasts, Uterus, Bladder, Bowel, Lochia, Episiotomy, Homans (calf), Emotions.

cards.q: What should be assessed in the baby at a postnatal home visit?
cards.a:
• Re-examine and chart in **Buku Rekod Kesihatan Bayi** (mother and clinic copies)
• **Weight**, **temperature**
• **Jaundice** (blanching test)
• **Feeding technique**; promote **early exclusive breastfeeding**
• **Warmth**, **hygienic cord and skin care**
• Counsel **when to bring the baby to a health facility**

cards.q: How is the blanching test for neonatal jaundice done and when is jaundice worrying?
cards.a:
• Press the skin (forehead, nose, sternum) with a finger and look for **yellow colour on blanching** in good daylight
• Jaundice spreads **head to toe** (cephalocaudal): below the umbilicus or to palms/soles suggests a high level
• **Jaundice within 24 hours of birth** is **pathological** → **urgent referral** for serum bilirubin
cards.m: Jaundice on day 1 = danger; day 3-5 = usually physiological.

cards.q: Baby blues versus postnatal depression: how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **Baby blues**: tearfulness, mood swings from about **day 3-5**, **resolves by day 10-14**; reassurance and support
• **Postnatal depression**: low mood/anhedonia **persisting beyond 2 weeks**, guilt, poor bonding, **suicidal thoughts**
• Screen with **EPDS**; persistent blues after day 10 need assessment
• Psychosis (confusion, hallucinations) = **emergency**
cards.m: Blues fade in 2 weeks; depression stays.

cards.q: Why is calf pain asked about at every postnatal visit?
cards.a:
• The puerperium is a **hypercoagulable** state: **VTE risk is highest in the first 6 weeks**, especially after caesarean
• Unilateral calf pain/swelling = **suspected DVT**
• Breathlessness or chest pain = **suspected PE**
• Both need **immediate hospital referral**

cards.q: Describe the normal progression of lochia and its warning signs.
cards.a:
• **Lochia rubra** (red): days 1-4
• **Lochia serosa** (pink-brown): to about day 10
• **Lochia alba** (yellow-white): up to 6 weeks
• Warning: **foul smell + fever + uterine tenderness** → **endometritis/puerperal sepsis**
• Fresh heavy bleeding after 24 h → **secondary PPH** (retained products, infection)
cards.m: Red, Serous, White - Rubra, Serosa, Alba.

cards.q: What is assessed in mother and baby at the postnatal clinic visit?
cards.a:
• **Mother**: general wellbeing, **PV bleeding/discharge**, urinary and bowel function, **wound and perineal healing**
• **Baby**: feeding, urinary and bowel activity, **anthropometry**, physical examination, **developmental assessment**, **immunisation**
• Common clinic tasks: **BP review**, **laboratory tests**, referral to MO, specific complaints

cards.q: What follow-up does a mother with gestational diabetes need after delivery?
cards.a:
• **75 g OGTT** between **6 weeks (42 days) and 3 months** postpartum
• Why: GDM women have a high lifetime risk of **type 2 diabetes**; persistent diabetes must be detected
• Then **annual glucose screening**, lifestyle advice and **pre-pregnancy care** before the next pregnancy
cards.m: GDM: test at 6 weeks to 3 months, then yearly for life.

cards.q: Which postnatal mothers are not eligible for virtual consultation?
cards.a:
• Suitability assessed on **day 5** by the **nurse during the home visit**
• Not eligible: **high-risk mothers and babies**
• Mothers with **yellow or red postnatal coding**
• Mothers with **social issues**
• Mothers with **poor compliance**

cards.q: What do the red and yellow postnatal codes mean? How does yellow differ from the antenatal yellow code?
cards.a:
• **Red**: **immediate referral to hospital**
• **Postnatal yellow**: **referral to a Medical Officer / Family Medicine Specialist**
• **Antenatal yellow**: referral for management by **hospital O&G specialist / FMS**
• Any abnormality → refer to clinic or hospital **according to the risk checklist**
cards.m: Postnatal yellow stays in the KK (MO/FMS).

cards.q: Give examples of postnatal problems that warrant a red code (immediate hospital referral).
cards.a:
• **Postpartum haemorrhage** / heavy fresh bleeding
• **Fits** or **severe hypertension** with symptoms
• **Puerperal sepsis** (fever, foul lochia, tachycardia)
• **Breathlessness/chest pain** (PE) or suspected **DVT**
• **Postpartum psychosis** or **suicidal ideation**
cards.m: Bleed, Fit, Fever, Breath, Mind.

cards.q: What counselling and follow-up are given at the postnatal clinic visit?
cards.a:
• **Birth spacing and family planning** - contraceptive options
• **Resumption of sexual intercourse**
• **Follow-up of mothers with medical conditions** (e.g. hypertension, diabetes)
• **GDM**: arrange the postnatal OGTT

cards.q: When should menses return after a miscarriage, and what advice is given?
cards.a:
• Next menses usually in **4-6 weeks**
• First period **may not be of normal volume or duration**
• **Record menses** to check regularity **before planning to conceive**

cards.q: What advice on activity and diet is given after miscarriage?
cards.a:
• **Avoid strenuous activities** initially
• **Well-balanced diet**
• **Appropriate fluid intake**

cards.q: When can sexual relations resume after miscarriage?
cards.a:
• After **vaginal bleeding stops**
• And any **perineal wound/stitches have healed**
• Why: reduces risk of **ascending infection** while the cervix is open and the endometrium heals

cards.q: What contraception advice is given after a miscarriage?
cards.a:
• **Avoid pregnancy soon** after miscarriage: counsel on **birth spacing and family planning**
• Ovulation can return within **2 weeks**, so start contraception **immediately**
• All methods can start straight away after first-trimester loss; **IUD can be inserted immediately** unless there is **sepsis**
cards.m: Fertility returns before the first period does.

cards.q: Which Rhesus-negative women need anti-D after miscarriage?
cards.a:
• Rh-negative, non-sensitised women with:
• Miscarriage **at or after 12 weeks**
• **Surgical evacuation** at any gestation
• **Ectopic pregnancy** or termination
• Give anti-D **within 72 hours**
cards.m: 12 weeks, surgery, ectopic → anti-D within 72 h.

cards.q: What emotional support and advice on the next pregnancy are given after miscarriage?
cards.a:
• **Counselling**: grief is normal; reassure that most losses are **chromosomal** and not caused by her
• Embark on the next pregnancy **when the couple is ready**
• It can proceed as long as the mother has **no medical illness** needing optimisation
• Investigate after **≥3 consecutive miscarriages**

cards.q: How is a woman who should avoid future pregnancy managed in postpartum pre-pregnancy care?
cards.a:
• Who: **serious medical conditions** where another pregnancy could **threaten her life** (e.g. pulmonary hypertension, severe heart failure)
• **Counsel the woman and partner**
• Provide **appropriate, highly effective contraception** (e.g. LARC, sterilisation)

cards.q: How are women likely to have high-risk future pregnancies managed after delivery?
cards.a:
• **Advise on risks** related to the current condition
• Encourage **pre-pregnancy care** and **use of contraception** until optimised
• **Enrol in pre-pregnancy care** at hospital or clinic **after the postnatal period**

cards.q: Define family planning and state its clinical goal.
cards.a:
• A **comprehensive approach** enabling individuals and couples to make **informed decisions** about reproductive health, incl. **number and spacing of children**
• Goal: improve **maternal and child health** by **preventing unintended pregnancy** and safely managing **medical eligibility**
• Birth control = devices, medications and procedures to prevent pregnancy

cards.q: What do UKMEC categories 1-4 mean?
cards.a:
• **1**: **no restriction** on use
• **2**: advantages **generally outweigh** risks
• **3**: risks **usually outweigh** advantages - use only with specialist judgement when nothing else is acceptable
• **4**: **unacceptable health risk** - do not use
cards.m: 1 Go, 2 Generally go, 3 Generally don't, 4 Don't.

cards.q: What are the five groups of contraceptive methods?
cards.a:
• **Barrier**: male/female condoms, cervical cap, diaphragm, spermicide
• **Hormonal**: pills, injections, implants
• **IUD**: copper (non-hormonal), levonorgestrel (hormonal)
• **Surgical**: bilateral tubal ligation, vasectomy
• **Natural**: calendar, basal body temperature, cervical mucus, lactational amenorrhoea
cards.m: B-H-I-S-N: Barrier, Hormones, IUD, Surgery, Nature.

cards.q: How does the combined oral contraceptive (COC) work, and what are its benefits and side effects?
cards.a:
• Action: **suppresses ovulation**, **thickens cervical mucus**, **endometrial atrophy**
• Benefits: accessible, effective, safe; improves **dysmenorrhoea and irregular menses**
• Side effects: **nausea, breast tenderness, headache**, amenorrhoea
• Needs **strict daily timing**

cards.q: List the contraindications to COC shown on the slides.
cards.a:
• **Breastfeeding <6 weeks** postpartum
• **Postpartum <21 days** (non-breastfeeding)
• **Breast cancer**
• History of **VTE or stroke**
• **Migraine with aura**
• **Smokers** (aged ≥35)
cards.m: Oestrogen hates clots, aura, cancer and cigarettes.

cards.q: List the UKMEC 4 conditions for combined hormonal contraception.
cards.a:
• **<6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding**; **<21 days** postpartum non-breastfeeding
• **Age ≥35 smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day**
• **BP ≥160/100** or vascular disease
• **Current or past VTE**, known **thrombogenic mutation**, major surgery with prolonged immobilisation
• **Migraine with aura**, **ischaemic heart disease, stroke**
• **Current breast cancer**; complicated valvular disease; SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies

cards.q: How do smoking and age affect eligibility for the combined pill (UKMEC)?
cards.a:
• **<35 years**, any smoking: **UKMEC 2**
• **≥35 years**, **<15/day**: **UKMEC 3**
• **≥35 years**, **≥15/day**: **UKMEC 4**
• **≥35**, stopped **<1 year** ago: **UKMEC 3**; stopped ≥1 year: UKMEC 2
cards.m: 35 and 15: over 35 smoking 15 = forbidden.

cards.q: What are the blood pressure cut-offs for using the combined pill (UKMEC)?
cards.a:
• **Adequately controlled hypertension**: **UKMEC 3**
• **Systolic 140-159 or diastolic 90-99**: **UKMEC 3**
• **Systolic ≥160 or diastolic ≥100**: **UKMEC 4**
• Hypertension **with vascular disease**: UKMEC 4
• Progestogen-only methods are UKMEC 1-2 → better choice

cards.q: How does migraine affect choice of contraception?
cards.a:
• **Migraine with aura** (any age): COC **UKMEC 4** - oestrogen adds to **ischaemic stroke** risk
• **Migraine without aura**: COC **UKMEC 2** to start (3 if it develops on COC)
• Progestogen-only methods and Cu-IUD are suitable
cards.m: Aura = alarm: no oestrogen.

cards.q: How does the progestogen-only pill (POP) work, and what are its side effects and contraindications?
cards.a:
• Action: makes cervical mucus **scanty and thick** (reduced volume, increased viscosity); **desogestrel suppresses ovulation**
• Note: slide p35 says it 'increases volume' of mucus - correct is **reduced volume, increased viscosity**
• Side effects: **acne, mood change, functional ovarian cysts**, breast tenderness, headache, nausea
• Contraindications: **breast cancer**, **severe liver disease**
• Suitable in **breastfeeding**

cards.q: Summarise the progestogen-only injectable (DMPA, Depo-Provera).
cards.a:
• Action: **thickens cervical mucus**, **thins endometrium** (and suppresses ovulation)
• Given every **12 weeks** (up to 13 weeks)
• Side effects: **irregular bleeding**, **weight gain**, **reduced bone mineral density**
• **Delayed return of fertility** (up to about 1 year) - avoid if pregnancy wanted soon
• Slide contraindications: **breastfeeding <6 weeks**, **breast cancer**, **osteoporosis**
cards.m: Depo = Delay (fertility) + Density (bone) + Dough (weight).

cards.q: Summarise the contraceptive implant.
cards.a:
• Action: **suppresses ovulation**, thickens cervical mucus
• **Highly effective** (>99%), **long-acting** (etonogestrel implant 3 years); does not affect intercourse
• Main side effect: **irregular spotting**
• Contraindications: **breast cancer**, **severe liver disease**

cards.q: Summarise the copper IUD (Cu-IUD).
cards.a:
• Action: **copper ions are toxic to sperm**; also **prevents implantation**
• Benefits: effective, safe, **cost-effective**, **non-hormonal**, few follow-ups; lasts **5-10 years**
• Side effects: **heavier menstrual bleeding**, **dysmenorrhoea**, spotting
• Contraindications: **active PID/STI**, **unexplained vaginal bleeding**, **Wilson's disease**, **copper allergy**
cards.m: Copper = heavier, crampier periods.

cards.q: Summarise the levonorgestrel IUD (LNG-IUS).
cards.a:
• Action: **local progestogen** - **thickens cervical mucus**, **thins endometrium**
• Note: slide p36 says 'thicken cervical wall' - correct is **cervical mucus**
• Side effects: **amenorrhoea** (often welcomed), spotting, pelvic pain, **ovarian cysts**
• Contraindications: **active PID/STI**, **unexplained vaginal bleeding**, **breast cancer**, **uterine anomalies**
• Useful for **heavy menstrual bleeding**
cards.m: Copper makes periods heavier; LNG makes them lighter.

cards.q: What are the features of the male condom?
cards.a:
• Physical barrier preventing sperm entering the vagina
• **Easy, cheap, universally accessible**
• **The only method with high STI protection**
• Side effects: **breakage/slippage**, skin irritation
• **Severe latex allergy**: use **polyurethane/polyisoprene** condoms
cards.m: Condom = the only contraceptive that also protects against STIs.

cards.q: Summarise surgical contraception (bilateral tubal ligation and vasectomy).
cards.a:
• **Permanent**, highly effective and safe
• Contraindicated if **any desire for future fertility** or **local infection**
• Vasectomy is **not immediately effective**: use backup until **semen analysis confirms azoospermia** (about 3 months)
• Counsel carefully: **regret** is commoner in young women and after recent delivery

cards.q: What are natural family planning methods and the criteria for the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM)?
cards.a:
• Natural: **calendar**, **basal body temperature**, **cervical mucus**, **lactational amenorrhoea**
• LAM is about **98% effective** only if ALL three:
• **Fully/nearly exclusive breastfeeding** (day and night)
• **Amenorrhoeic**
• Baby **<6 months** old
cards.m: LAM needs all 3: Lactating fully, Amenorrhoeic, Months <6.

cards.q: When can a woman start the COC in relation to her menstrual cycle?
cards.a:
• **Within the first 5 days** of the period: **no backup** needed
• **>5 days** into the cycle: start anytime if **not pregnant** + **7 days backup** (condom/abstinence)
• **Amenorrhoeic**: start anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup**
cards.m: COC: 5 days to start, 7 days to cover.

cards.q: When can a woman start the POP in relation to her menstrual cycle?
cards.a:
• **Within the first 5 days** of the period: no backup
• **>5 days**: start anytime if not pregnant + **2 days (48 hours) backup**
• **Amenorrhoeic**: start anytime if not pregnant + **2 days backup**
• Why only 2 days: the mucus effect is established within 48 h
cards.m: POP = 2 days; COC = 7 days.

cards.q: When can the progestogen-only injectable be started in the cycle?
cards.a:
• **Within the first 7 days** of the period: no backup
• **>7 days**: inject anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup / abstinence**
• **Amenorrhoeic**: inject anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup**

cards.q: When can the COC be started after delivery?
cards.a:
• **Breastfeeding**: **<6 weeks contraindicated**; **6 weeks-6 months** (exclusive BF) **not recommended unless no alternative**; **>6 months** start as a regular/amenorrhoeic user
• **Not breastfeeding**: **<21 days not recommended** (VTE risk); **≥21 days** start if no VTE risk factors (+ 7 days backup if amenorrhoeic)
• Why: postpartum **hypercoagulability** and oestrogen's effect on **milk supply**
cards.m: COC postpartum: 21 days if bottle-feeding, 6 weeks (really 6 months) if breastfeeding.

cards.q: When can progestogen-only methods (POP, injectable, implant) be started after delivery?
cards.a:
• **POP**: **safe <6 weeks** breastfeeding; non-BF <21 days no backup; ≥21 days + 2 days backup
• **Implant**: **can be inserted <6 weeks**; non-BF <21 days no backup
• **Injectable**: breastfeeding **<6 weeks not recommended unless no other method**; 6 weeks-6 months (exclusive BF, amenorrhoeic) inject without backup; non-BF <21 days without backup

cards.q: When can implants be started in the menstrual cycle?
cards.a:
• **Within the first 7 days** of the period (**first 5 days** for etonogestrel 68 mg): no backup
• Beyond this window: insert anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup/abstinence**
• **Amenorrhoeic**: insert anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup**

cards.q: When can a Cu-IUD versus an LNG-IUD be inserted in the menstrual cycle?
cards.a:
• **Cu-IUD**: within **first 12 days** - no backup; after 12 days or amenorrhoeic: insert anytime if not pregnant - **no backup ever needed** (copper works immediately)
• **LNG-IUD**: within **first 7 days** - no backup; after 7 days or amenorrhoeic: insert anytime if not pregnant + **7 days backup**
cards.m: Copper is instant; hormone needs a week.

cards.q: When can an IUD be inserted after delivery?
cards.a:
• **<48 hours**: right **after placental delivery** or **during caesarean before uterine closure**
• **48 hours to <4 weeks**: **not recommended** (higher **expulsion/perforation** risk)
• **≥4 weeks**: insert anytime once **pregnancy excluded**
• Same for breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding
• **Contraindicated in puerperal sepsis**
cards.m: IUD after birth: 2 days or 4 weeks - nothing in between.

cards.q: Which contraceptives are affected by enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin)?
cards.a:
• **Reduced efficacy**: **COC, POP, implant** (and LNG emergency pill)
• **Unaffected**: **Cu-IUD**, **LNG-IUS**, **DMPA injection**
• Advise a **non-enzyme-dependent method** during and for **28 days after** stopping the inducer
cards.m: Inducers eat pills and rods, not coils or jabs.

cards.q: What is the Islamic perspective on family planning taught in the seminar?
cards.a:
• **Tanzim al-nasl** (planning/spacing children, e.g. pills, IUD): **permissible** if the couple accepts a child as Allah's gift, it is **not harmful** (especially to the wife) and **both spouses consent**
• **Tahdid al-nasl** (permanent sterilisation: vasectomy, BTL): **prohibited** as changing Allah's creation, except in circumstances **permitted by syarak** (e.g. medical necessity)

cards.q: What are the emergency contraception options in order of effectiveness?
cards.a:
• **Cu-IUD**: **most effective (>99%)**
• **Ulipristal acetate (UPA) 30 mg**
• **Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg**
• **Combined (Yuzpe)** regimen: least effective, most nausea
• Always offer the Cu-IUD first if acceptable
cards.m: Coil > Ulipristal > Levonorgestrel > Yuzpe (C-U-L-Y).

cards.q: What is the time window for a copper IUD as emergency contraception?
cards.a:
• Within **5 days (120 hours)** of the **first** unprotected intercourse
• **Or** up to **5 days after the earliest estimated ovulation** (even if several UPSI episodes)
• Works independent of body weight and drug interactions

cards.q: What is the key advantage of the Cu-IUD over emergency pills?
cards.a:
• **Does NOT need to be removed after menses**
• Provides **long-term continuous contraception** (5-10 years)
• **Most effective** EC; not affected by **BMI** or **enzyme inducers**
• Pills only cover that single episode

cards.q: Ulipristal acetate (UPA) as emergency contraception: dose, window and key points.
cards.a:
• **30 mg single dose** stat, within **120 hours (5 days)**
• Delays ovulation even **after the LH surge has started** - more effective than LNG
• **MEC 2 in breastfeeding** (FSRH advises expressing and discarding milk for 1 week)
• Not recommended with **enzyme inducers**; efficacy reduced if progestogen started within 5 days

cards.q: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception: dose and time window.
cards.a:
• **LNG 1.5 mg single dose** (or 0.75 mg twice, 12 hours apart)
• Licensed and most effective **within 72 hours**; effectiveness falls with time
• Note: slide p39 says 'within 120 hours' - WHO allows use up to 120 h, but beyond **72 h** prefer **UPA or Cu-IUD**
• Can start hormonal contraception **immediately** after LNG
cards.m: LNG = 3 days; UPA and copper = 5 days.

cards.q: What is the combined (Yuzpe) emergency contraception regimen?
cards.a:
• **Ethinyl oestradiol 100 µg + LNG 0.5 mg** stat
• **Repeated after 12 hours**
• Least effective and most **nausea/vomiting**; use only when UPA/LNG unavailable

cards.q: How should ongoing hormonal contraception be started after emergency pills?
cards.a:
• After **LNG**: start **immediately** + backup (7 days COC/implant/injection, 2 days POP)
• After **UPA**: **wait 5 days** before starting hormonal contraception (progestogen blocks UPA), then add usual backup
• Use condoms/abstain meanwhile
cards.m: UPA: wait 5 days before the pill.

cards.q: How do body weight and enzyme inducers alter the choice of emergency contraception?
cards.a:
• **BMI >26 or weight >70 kg**: LNG less effective → offer **Cu-IUD**, or **UPA**, or **double-dose LNG 3 mg**
• **Enzyme inducers** (or within 28 days of stopping): **Cu-IUD preferred**; otherwise **LNG 3 mg**; UPA not recommended

cards.q: What follow-up and counselling points accompany emergency contraceptive pills?
cards.a:
• Works mainly by **delaying ovulation** - **not an abortifacient**; does not harm an established pregnancy
• Does **not protect** against later UPSI in the same cycle
• **Vomiting within 3 hours**: repeat the dose
• **Pregnancy test at 3 weeks** if next period is late, light or abnormal
• Offer **STI screening** and ongoing contraception

cards.q: What should a woman do if she misses one combined pill (1-2 days late, i.e. 24-48 hours)?
cards.a:
• **Take the missed pill as soon as possible** (even 2 pills in one day)
• **Continue the rest of the pack** as usual
• **No backup** and **no emergency contraception** needed
cards.m: One missed COC = just catch up.

cards.q: What should a woman do if she misses two or more combined pills (>48 hours late)?
cards.a:
• Take the **most recent missed pill ASAP** (discard the others) and continue the pack
• Use **condoms/abstain for 7 days**
• **Missed in week 3**: finish active pills, **omit the hormone-free interval**, start the **next pack immediately**
• **Missed in week 1 + UPSI** (in that week or the pill-free interval): **consider EC**
• Note: slide p40 omits the **7-day backup** - it is required
cards.m: 2 missed = 7 days cover; week 1 = EC; week 3 = skip the break.

cards.q: What are the missed-pill rules for the progestogen-only pill?
cards.a:
• Late **<3 hours** (**<12 hours for desogestrel**): take ASAP, continue, no backup
• Late **>3 hours** (**>12 h desogestrel**): take ASAP, continue, **backup for 2 days**
• **EC needed** if UPSI occurred after the missed pill and before 2 days of correct use
cards.m: POP: 3 hours (12 for desogestrel), then 2 days of cover.

cards.q: Why is the pill-free week the most dangerous time to miss combined pills?
cards.a:
• During the **7-day hormone-free interval** the ovary starts to recover
• Extending it (missing pills in **week 1** or **late week 3**) beyond 7 days allows **follicle development and ovulation**
• Hence: week 1 misses → consider EC; week 3 misses → **skip the break**

cards.q: Define pre-pregnancy care.
cards.a:
• Provision of **biomedical, behavioural and social** health interventions to **women and couples before conception**
• Aims to **improve health status** and reduce behaviours and individual/environmental factors that lead to **poor maternal and child outcomes**

cards.q: Who are the target groups for pre-pregnancy care?
cards.a:
• Women of **reproductive age (15-49 years)** with:
• **Chronic disease**
• **Infectious disease**
• **Lifestyle risks**: smoking, alcohol, substance abuse, obesity

cards.q: Where are pre-pregnancy care services offered in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **O&G specialist clinics**
• **Health clinics** (Klinik Kesihatan)
• **Outpatient services at district hospitals**

cards.q: What are the four steps of the pre-pregnancy care process?
cards.a:
• **1. Identification and referral**: screen for risk factors; refer directly to MO
• **2. Assessment**: history, examination, lab tests, pregnancy intention, suitability
• **3. Management**: optimise risk, **start folic acid**, family planning, education, counselling
• **4. Follow-up**: shared care; **reassess fitness** for pregnancy
cards.m: I-A-M-F: Identify, Assess, Manage, Follow up.

cards.q: What does the pre-pregnancy assessment of a client include?
cards.a:
• **History** and **physical examination**
• **Clinical laboratory tests**
• Explore **pregnancy intention and plan**
• **Assess suitability for pregnancy**
• Fill the **first assessment form**

cards.q: What management is offered in pre-pregnancy care once risks are identified?
cards.a:
• **Optimise** medical and biopsychosocial risks
• **Initiate folic acid**
• Provide **family planning** if pregnancy should be delayed
• **Health education** and **counselling**

cards.q: What does follow-up in pre-pregnancy care involve?
cards.a:
• **Establish follow-up**
• **Shared care** in preparation for pregnancy, especially for **poorly optimised** conditions
• **Reassess fitness for pregnancy** in certain medical conditions before stopping contraception

cards.q: Which chronic medical conditions are pre-pregnancy risk factors?
cards.a:
• **Hypertension**, **heart disease**, **diabetes**, **thyroid disease**
• **Epilepsy**, **asthma**, **connective tissue disease (SLE)**
• **Renal** and **blood disorders**, **malignancy**, **transplant**
• **Mental illness** (mood disorder, schizophrenia)

cards.q: Which age, lifestyle, social and family factors are pre-pregnancy risk factors?
cards.a:
• **Age**: teenage (**<18**) or advanced maternal age (**>35**)
• **Lifestyle**: smoking, substance abuse, high-risk sexual behaviour, **obesity/underweight**, pets (toxoplasmosis)
• **Social**: **domestic violence**, low socioeconomic status, marginalised groups, single mothers
• **Family**: **congenital structural abnormalities**
cards.m: Under 18 or over 35 = age risk.

cards.q: Folic acid before pregnancy: who gets 0.4 mg and who needs 5 mg?
cards.a:
• **0.4 mg daily** for all women planning pregnancy, ideally **from ≥3 months before conception** until **12 weeks**
• **5 mg daily** (high risk of neural tube defect):
• **Previous NTD** baby or family history
• On **antiepileptic drugs**
• **Diabetes**
• **BMI ≥30**
• **Thalassaemia/sickle cell**, malabsorption (coeliac)
cards.m: High-dose 5 for: NTD, Epilepsy, Diabetes, Obesity, Thalassaemia (NEDOT).

cards.q: Which teratogenic drugs should be switched before conception, and to what?
cards.a:
• **ACE inhibitors / ARBs** → **labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa**
• **Warfarin** (embryopathy 6-12 weeks) → specialist plan, usually **LMWH**
• **Valproate** (NTD, neurodevelopmental harm) → specialist switch (e.g. **lamotrigine/levetiracetam**); never stop abruptly
• **Statins** → stop; **methotrexate** → stop ≥3 months before; **isotretinoin** → stop and wait 1 month
cards.m: AWVS-MI: ACEi, Warfarin, Valproate, Statin, Methotrexate, Isotretinoin.

cards.q: What pre-pregnancy glycaemic targets are advised for women with diabetes?
cards.a:
• Aim **HbA1c <6.5%** before conception if achievable without hypoglycaemia
• **HbA1c >10%**: **avoid pregnancy** (high risk of **congenital anomalies** and miscarriage) - use effective contraception until optimised
• Switch to **insulin ± metformin**; stop other oral agents
• **Folic acid 5 mg**; screen for **retinopathy and nephropathy**
cards.m: 6.5 to go, 10 says no.

cards.q: How is rubella immunity handled in pre-pregnancy care?
cards.a:
• Check **rubella IgG** (or vaccination history) before conception
• Non-immune: give **MMR** and advise to **avoid pregnancy for 1 month (28 days)** afterwards
• Why: congenital rubella syndrome (**cataract, deafness, cardiac defects**) is greatest in the first trimester
cards.m: MMR then a month's wait.

cards.q: What pre-pregnancy advice is given to a woman on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism?
cards.a:
• Optimise to a **TSH within the trimester-appropriate range** (aim <2.5 mIU/L) before conception
• Once pregnancy is confirmed, **increase the dose by about 25-30%** (e.g. 2 extra tablets per week) and recheck TFT in 4-6 weeks
• Why: fetal brain development depends on **maternal thyroxine** in the first trimester

cards.q: How common is cervical cancer globally and in Malaysia (per the slides)?
cards.a:
• Globally: **5th** most commonly diagnosed cancer in women (WHO)
• Malaysia: **3rd most common cancer in women** (MOH 2023)
• Largely **preventable** by HPV vaccination and screening

cards.q: What causes cervical cancer?
cards.a:
• **Persistent infection with high-risk HPV**, mainly **types 16 and 18** (about 70% of cases)
• Infection at the **transformation zone** → CIN → invasive cancer over **10-15 years**
• Risk factors: early sexual debut, multiple partners, **smoking**, **HIV/immunosuppression**, never screened
cards.m: No persistent HPV, (almost) no cervical cancer.

cards.q: What are the cervical screening methods in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Cytology-based (Pap smear)**: **conventional** cytology or **liquid-based cytology (LBC)**
• **HPV DNA test** (provider or **self-sampling**)

cards.q: Who is screened with cytology and who with an HPV test (Malaysian guideline 2023)?
cards.a:
• **Cytology**: women **<30 years** (sexually active, from about age 20)
• **HPV test**: **sexually active women 30-65 years**
• Also HPV test for women **>65** who **never had routine screening**
cards.m: Under 30 = cells (Pap); 30-65 = virus (HPV).

cards.q: What are the cervical screening intervals?
cards.a:
• **Cytology**: **yearly for 2 years**; if both normal → **3-yearly**
• **HPV test negative**: repeat **every 5 years**
• **HPV positive**: manage according to the HPV result algorithm
cards.m: Pap 1-1-3; HPV 5.

cards.q: Why is HPV testing used from age 30 but not in younger women?
cards.a:
• HPV test is **more sensitive** than cytology → safe **5-yearly** interval
• Under 30, HPV infection is **common and usually transient** (cleared within 1-2 years)
• HPV testing in young women causes **over-referral** and unnecessary colposcopy

cards.q: What instruments are needed for a Pap smear?
cards.a:
• **Cusco bivalve speculum**, gloves, swabs, **normal saline**, couch and privacy screen
• Samplers: **cervical broom (Cervex-Brush Combi)**, **endocervical brush**, **spatula**
• **HPV/cytology request form**
• Conventional: **frosted-end slide + 2B pencil** (or diamond pencil), **95% ethyl alcohol fixative**, slide mailer
• LBC: **preservative vial**

cards.q: Conventional Pap smear versus liquid-based cytology (LBC): what is the practical difference?
cards.a:
• **Conventional**: cells smeared on a **glass slide** and **fixed immediately** with alcohol
• **LBC**: sampler head rinsed into a **preservative vial**
• LBC: fewer **unsatisfactory** samples and allows **reflex HPV testing** on the same sample

cards.q: How is the patient prepared for a Pap smear?
cards.a:
• **Explain** purpose and procedure
• Obtain **informed consent**
• Ensure **privacy and comfort**: screen/curtain, **chaperone**
• Position: **dorsal lithotomy**

cards.q: What advice is given before collecting a Pap smear?
cards.a:
• **Avoid** sampling during **menstruation**
• **No sexual intercourse for 48 hours** before
• **No douching, vaginal medication or tampons for 48 hours** before
• Can be done from **6 weeks postpartum**
• If a **cervical lesion is seen** → **refer to a gynaecologist**
cards.m: 48 hours: no sex, no douche, no pessary.

cards.q: Outline the steps of performing a Pap smear.
cards.a:
• **Hand hygiene**, gloves and apron; **dorsal lithotomy**
• **Inspect** vulva for lesions/discharge
• Wet the **Cusco speculum with normal saline** and insert
• **Visualise the cervix and the transformation zone**
• Sample with the appropriate device; transfer to slide/vial
• **Label** and send with the completed request form

cards.q: What is the transformation zone and why must it be sampled?
cards.a:
• Area between the **original and new squamocolumnar junction** where columnar epithelium undergoes **squamous metaplasia**
• Metaplastic cells are most vulnerable to **HPV-driven dysplasia** - **most CIN and cancers arise here**
• Moves **inward (into the canal) after menopause** → endocervical brush needed

cards.q: How should a conventional smear be spread and fixed, and why?
cards.a:
• Smear the sample **in one direction** on the glass slide (thin even layer)
• **Fix with alcohol spray within 5 seconds**
• Why: **air-drying artefact** distorts cells and makes the smear **unsatisfactory**
cards.m: One stroke, five seconds.

cards.q: What are the two HPV test sampling approaches?
cards.a:
• **Self-sampling**: the woman collects a vaginal swab herself - improves uptake (privacy, no speculum)
• **Provider sampling**: assisted sampling for women **not confident** to self-sample
• Provider sampling is done in the **supine position without a speculum**

cards.q: How are HPV test results managed (Malaysian guideline)?
cards.a:
• **HPV negative** → routine re-screen in **5 years**
• **HPV 16/18 positive** → **refer for colposcopy**
• **Other high-risk HPV positive** → **reflex cytology (LBC)**:
• cytology **≥ASCUS** → **colposcopy**
• cytology **normal** → **repeat HPV test in 12 months**
cards.m: 16/18 go straight to the scope.

cards.q: How are abnormal cytology (Pap) results managed?
cards.a:
• **Unsatisfactory**: **repeat in about 3 months** (after treating any infection)
• **ASC-US**: **HPV triage** (positive → colposcopy) or **repeat cytology in 6-12 months**
• **LSIL**: **colposcopy**
• **ASC-H, HSIL, AGC, suspected cancer**: **colposcopy** (urgent)
• Any **visible lesion**: refer gynaecology regardless of smear
cards.m: Undetermined → triage; any lesion called L, H or glandular → colposcope.

cards.q: What should be done for a woman with post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding who had a normal smear last year?
cards.a:
• Screening tests are for **asymptomatic** women - **do not rely on a previous normal smear**
• Perform **speculum examination**
• Refer to **gynaecology** for assessment (colposcopy) if the cervix looks abnormal or bleeding persists
• Exclude infection (chlamydia) and pregnancy

cards.q: What are the key facts about HPV vaccination in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• School-based **National Immunisation Programme** for **13-year-old girls** (Form 1)
• Best given **before sexual debut**; protects against **HPV 16/18** (≈70% of cervical cancers)
• **Vaccinated women still need screening** - vaccine does not cover all oncogenic types

cards.q: How common is breast cancer globally and in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Globally: **1st** most common cancer in women; **2nd** among all cancers (GLOBOCAN 2024)
• Malaysia: **1st** most common cancer in women **and** among all cancers

cards.q: What are the breast cancer screening methods and target groups?
cards.a:
• **Screening mammogram** (without contrast): women **50-74 years**
• **Clinical breast examination (CBE)**: women **from 35 years**
• Plus **breast self-awareness** at all ages
cards.m: CBE from 35; mammogram 50-74.

cards.q: What are the general breast screening intervals?
cards.a:
• Women **50-74**: screening mammogram **biennially (2-yearly)**
• Women **≥35, asymptomatic**: interval **depends on risk assessment** (average, moderate, high)

cards.q: How is an average-risk woman defined and screened?
cards.a:
• **Average risk**: **<17% lifetime risk**
• **40-49 years**: screening mammography **annually** (per slide)
• **50-74 years**: screening mammography **biennially**

cards.q: How is a moderate-risk woman defined and screened?
cards.a:
• **Moderate risk**: **>17% but <30% lifetime risk** (e.g. one first-degree relative diagnosed young)
• **40-49**: mammography **annually**
• **50-59**: **annually or biennially**
• **≥60**: **3-yearly**
cards.m: 17 and 30 are the risk fences.

cards.q: How is a high-risk woman without a known genetic variant screened?
cards.a:
• **High risk**: **>30% lifetime risk**, no known pathogenic variant
• **30-39**: mammography **in consideration**
• **40-59**: mammography **annually**
• **≥60**: **3-yearly**

cards.q: How are BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 carriers (unaffected) screened?
cards.a:
• **30-49 years**: **MRI breast annually**
• **40-69 years**: **mammography annually**
• **≥70 years**: mammography **3-yearly**
• Refer for **genetic counselling** and discuss risk-reducing options
cards.m: Gene carriers start at 30 with MRI.

cards.q: What surveillance is advised for women with a personal history of breast cancer?
cards.a:
• With increased risk of recurrence/second cancer, **any age**: **mammography of remnant and contralateral breast annually for 5 years**
• **BRCA1/2 (no TP53)**, age **50-74**: **mammography annually**
• **BRCA1/2 or TP53**, age **30-49**: **MRI annually**
• **Dense breasts or diagnosed before 50**: **MRI annually**

cards.q: How are TP53 carriers and women with previous chest radiation screened?
cards.a:
• **TP53 mutation** (or >30% chance of being a carrier): **MRI breast annually from 20-69**
• **Chest radiation before age 30** (e.g. Hodgkin lymphoma): start at **age 25 or 8 years after radiation**, annually with **MRI**, **mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis**

cards.q: Why is MRI rather than mammography used for young high-risk and TP53 carriers?
cards.a:
• Young women have **dense breast tissue** → mammography is less sensitive
• **TP53 (Li-Fraumeni)** carriers are **radiation-sensitive** → avoid ionising radiation
• MRI has the **highest sensitivity** in BRCA carriers

cards.q: What is breast self-awareness and how should women practise it?
cards.a:
• Knowing what is **normal for her own breasts** and reporting changes **promptly**
• Look and feel regularly (e.g. monthly, **a week after menses**; any fixed day if postmenopausal)
• Changes to report: **lump, skin dimpling, nipple inversion, bloody discharge, axillary lump**
• Not a substitute for CBE/mammography
cards.m: TLC: Touch, Look, Check (report changes).

cards.q: What are the main risk factors for breast cancer?
cards.a:
• **Female sex, increasing age**
• **Family history** / **BRCA1/2**, previous breast cancer or atypical hyperplasia
• Long oestrogen exposure: **early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, first pregnancy >30, not breastfeeding**
• **Combined HRT**, **obesity (postmenopausal)**, **alcohol**, chest radiation

cards.q: Which breast symptoms need urgent referral and what is triple assessment?
cards.a:
• Red flags: **hard, irregular, fixed lump**, **skin tethering/peau d'orange**, **new nipple retraction**, **bloody nipple discharge**, **axillary lymph node**, non-healing nipple eczema
• Refer urgently to the **breast/surgical clinic**
• **Triple assessment**: **clinical examination + imaging** (ultrasound <35 y; mammogram + US ≥35 y) **+ tissue biopsy** (core needle)
cards.m: Triple = Feel, See, Sample.

cards.q: Which family history features suggest a woman may be at high (possibly genetic) risk and need referral for risk assessment?
cards.a:
• **First-degree relative** with breast cancer **<40 years**
• **Two or more** close relatives with breast or **ovarian cancer** on the same side
• **Male breast cancer** in the family
• **Bilateral** breast cancer in a relative
• **Known BRCA1/2, PALB2 or TP53** variant in the family
• Refer to breast/genetic clinic to estimate **lifetime risk** (<17%, 17-30%, >30%)

cards.q: Define menopause and state the average age in Malaysia.
cards.a:
• A definite phase when the **ovaries stop producing oestrogen** and **menstruation stops**; marks the **end of fertility**
• Natural menopause usually between **45 and 55 years** worldwide
• **Average age in Malaysia: 50.7 years**
cards.m: Malaysia ≈ 51.

cards.q: How is menopause diagnosed?
cards.a:
• Only after **12 full months of amenorrhoea**
• After **pathological or physiological causes** (pregnancy, lactation, thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia) are **ruled out**
• Therefore a **retrospective** diagnosis
cards.m: Menopause is diagnosed looking back 12 months.

cards.q: Distinguish natural menopause, perimenopause, menopausal transition, climacteric and premenopause.
cards.a:
• **Natural menopause**: permanent cessation from **loss of ovarian follicular activity**; no bleeding for 12 months
• **Menopausal transition**: **cycle variability** until the final period
• **Perimenopause**: just before menopause **until 1 year after the last period**
• **Climacteric**: the **longer** transition from reproductive to non-reproductive phase
• **Premenopause**: the **1-2 years** before menopause
cards.m: Peri = transition + 1 year after.

cards.q: What is the STRAW+10 classification?
cards.a:
• **Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop + 10**
• Depicts the natural transition from **reproductive years to menopause and postmenopause**
• Uses **menstrual cycle pattern** (main criterion) and **hormonal measurements** (FSH, AMH, antral follicle count) to define stages

cards.q: When is FSH testing needed to diagnose menopause?
cards.a:
• **Not needed** in women **>45 years** with **typical symptoms** - clinical diagnosis
• Consider FSH in women **40-45** with symptoms/changed periods
• **<40 years** with suspected POI: **FSH twice, 4-6 weeks apart**
• FSH is unreliable on **combined hormonal contraception** or high-dose progestogen
cards.m: Over 45 + flushes = no blood test.

cards.q: What is premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Loss of ovarian function **before 40 years**: amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea + **raised FSH on two occasions**
• Risks: **osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease**, infertility, psychological distress
• Treat with **HRT or COC until at least the average age of natural menopause** (about 51)
• Here HRT is **replacement**, not added risk

cards.q: What are the symptoms and long-term consequences of menopause?
cards.a:
• **Vasomotor**: **hot flushes, night sweats** (commonest)
• **Psychological**: low mood, anxiety, irritability, poor concentration, **sleep disturbance**
• **Genitourinary syndrome**: vaginal dryness, **dyspareunia**, urgency, recurrent UTI
• Musculoskeletal: joint aches; reduced libido
• Long term: **osteoporosis/fractures**, **cardiovascular disease**
cards.m: Hot, Moody, Dry, Brittle.

cards.q: Why do hot flushes occur in menopause?
cards.a:
• **Oestrogen withdrawal** alters hypothalamic thermoregulation (via **KNDy neurons / neurokinin B**)
• The **thermoneutral zone narrows**, so a tiny rise in core temperature triggers **peripheral vasodilatation and sweating**
• Explains why **oestrogen** is the most effective treatment and why **fezolinetant** (NK3 antagonist) works

cards.q: How is genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vaginal atrophy) treated?
cards.a:
• **Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants** first
• **Low-dose vaginal oestrogen** (cream, pessary): effective, minimal systemic absorption
• Vaginal oestrogen **does not need a progestogen** even with a uterus
• Can be used **long term** and alongside systemic HRT

cards.q: What lifestyle advice helps menopausal women?
cards.a:
• **Regular exercise** (weight-bearing for bone), **weight control**
• **Stop smoking**, limit **alcohol** and **caffeine** (flush triggers)
• Layered clothing, cool bedroom, **sleep hygiene**
• **Calcium and vitamin D**-rich diet
• Screen cardiovascular risk (BP, lipids, glucose) and fracture risk

cards.q: What non-hormonal drugs can treat menopausal vasomotor symptoms?
cards.a:
• **SSRIs** (e.g. paroxetine, escitalopram)
• **SNRIs** (e.g. **venlafaxine**)
• **Clonidine**
• (Also gabapentin)
• Use when HRT is **contraindicated or declined**; less effective than oestrogen
cards.m: Non-hormonal trio: SSRI, SNRI, Clonidine.

cards.q: Which SSRIs should be avoided for hot flushes in women on tamoxifen, and why?
cards.a:
• Avoid **paroxetine and fluoxetine**
• They strongly **inhibit CYP2D6**, reducing conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite **endoxifen** → may **reduce anticancer effect**
• Prefer **venlafaxine** (or citalopram/escitalopram)

cards.q: What herbal products, supplements and alternative therapies are listed for menopause?
cards.a:
• **Herbal**: **isoflavones/phytoestrogens**, **red clover**, **soy**, **evening primrose oil** - evidence weak; quality and interactions vary
• **Supplements**: **vitamin D** (skeletal health), **calcium** (fracture risk reduction)
• **Alternative**: **hypnotherapy**, **relaxation techniques**, **sleep hygiene**

cards.q: What are the indications for menopausal hormone therapy (HRT)?
cards.a:
• **Moderate-severe vasomotor symptoms** affecting quality of life - most effective treatment
• **Premature ovarian insufficiency / early menopause** (until about 51)
• **Prevention of osteoporosis** in women **<60** at risk of fracture
• Genitourinary symptoms (vaginal oestrogen)

cards.q: Which HRT regimen: oestrogen-only or combined?
cards.a:
• **Hysterectomy**: **oestrogen-only** HRT
• **Uterus intact**: **oestrogen + progestogen** (combined)
• Why: **unopposed oestrogen** causes **endometrial hyperplasia and cancer**
• Progestogen may be oral, transdermal or **LNG-IUS**
cards.m: Uterus in = progestogen in.

cards.q: Cyclical (sequential) versus continuous combined HRT: who gets which?
cards.a:
• **Cyclical combined**: **perimenopausal** women still having periods or **LMP <12 months** ago - gives a monthly withdrawal bleed
• **Continuous combined**: **postmenopausal** (**>12 months** amenorrhoea, or after 1 year of cyclical HRT) - no bleeding
• Continuous combined in perimenopause causes **erratic bleeding**
cards.m: Still cycling → cyclical; stopped → continuous.

cards.q: What are the contraindications to systemic HRT?
cards.a:
• **Current, past or suspected breast cancer**
• **Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding** (investigate first)
• **Active or recent VTE** (oral HRT) or arterial disease (MI, stroke)
• **Active liver disease** with abnormal LFTs
• Known/suspected **oestrogen-dependent cancer** (e.g. untreated endometrial)
• **Pregnancy**; untreated endometrial hyperplasia
cards.m: BBC-LP: Breast cancer, Bleeding, Clots, Liver, Pregnancy.

cards.q: What are the main risks of HRT and how are they minimised?
cards.a:
• **VTE**: higher with **oral** oestrogen → use **transdermal** if VTE risk or BMI >30
• **Breast cancer**: small rise with **combined** HRT, related to duration; little or none with oestrogen-only
• **Stroke**: small rise with oral oestrogen
• Benefit greatest if started **<60 years or within 10 years of menopause**
• Review **annually**; lowest effective dose for symptoms

cards.q: How do WHO and the UN define violence and violence against women?
cards.a:
• **Violence (WHO)**: intentional use of **physical force or power**, threatened or actual, against oneself, another or a group, that results or is likely to result in **injury, death, psychological harm, maldevelopment or deprivation**
• **Violence against women (UN)**: any act of **gender-based violence** causing or likely to cause physical, sexual or mental harm, incl. **threats, coercion or arbitrary deprivation of liberty**, in **public or private** life

cards.q: What forms does intimate partner violence (IPV) take?
cards.a:
• **Physical** violence
• **Sexual** violence
• **Emotional/psychological** abuse
• **Controlling behaviour** (isolation from family, monitoring, restricting money or health care)
• Violence against women also includes **sexual assault** by non-partners
cards.m: PSEC: Physical, Sexual, Emotional, Controlling.

cards.q: How common is violence against women globally and in Malaysia (per the slides)?
cards.a:
• Globally about **1 in 3 women** have experienced partner or non-partner violence (WHO)
• **8%** of women >15 years (**263 million**) have experienced **non-partner sexual violence**
• Malaysia domestic violence cases: **5,507 (2023) → 7,116 (2024) → 7,391 (2025)** - rising

cards.q: What individual risk factors are linked to IPV and sexual violence?
cards.a:
• **Lower education** level
• **History of child abuse**; **witnessing family violence**
• **Poor mental health**
• **Harmful alcohol use**
• Belief that violence is **acceptable or normal**
• **Controlling behaviour** and **unequal power** in the relationship; multiple sexual relationships

cards.q: What community and societal factors increase violence against women?
cards.a:
• **Harmful gender norms** (men above women), **gender discrimination**
• **High poverty and unemployment**
• **High rates of child marriage**
• High **violence and crime**; easy access to **drugs, alcohol and weapons**
• **Unfair laws** (property, divorce, marriage) and **weak enforcement** of protective laws

cards.q: Which clinical presentations should make you suspect a woman is experiencing violence?
cards.a:
• **Injuries that are repeated or not well explained**
• **Ongoing emotional problems**, **self-harm** or suicidal thoughts
• **Repeated STIs** and **unwanted pregnancies**
• **Unexplained chronic pain** or conditions
• **Repeated consultations with no clear diagnosis**
• Partner who is intrusive, always present, answers for her
cards.m: Repeated visits + vague complaints = ask about safety at home.

cards.q: When giving first-line support to a woman experiencing violence, what do you NOT need to do?
cards.a:
• **Solve her problems**
• **Convince her to leave** the relationship
• **Convince her to go** to other services
• Ask **detailed questions** that make her **relive painful events**
• Ask her to **analyse what happened and why**
• **Pressure her** to tell you her feelings
cards.m: Support, don't rescue.

cards.q: What is the WHO 'LIVES' approach to first-line support?
cards.a:
• **L**isten: closely, with empathy, without judging
• **I**nquire about needs and concerns (emotional, physical, social, practical)
• **V**alidate: show you believe her; it is not her fault
• **E**nhance safety: discuss a plan to protect herself from further harm
• **S**upport: connect to services (OSCC, social welfare, NGOs, police)
cards.m: LIVES saves lives.

cards.q: How is immediate safety assessed in a woman disclosing IPV?
cards.a:
• Ask about **escalation** in frequency or severity
• **Weapons** in the home; **threats to kill**; **strangulation/choking**
• **Pregnancy**, **jealousy/controlling behaviour**, **children at risk**
• Any **yes** to several → **high risk**: make an **immediate safety plan** (safe place, emergency bag, numbers), OSCC/police/shelter
• Malaysia: **Talian Kasih 15999**, Women's Aid Organisation, **Domestic Violence Act 1994** protection orders

cards.q: How should a clinician ask about and document suspected domestic violence?
cards.a:
• Ask **in private**, **without the partner or family** present; use a **professional interpreter**, not relatives
• Ask **simply and directly** in a non-judgemental way
• Record her **own words**, date/time, **body chart** of injuries with size and colour, **photographs with consent**
• Keep records **confidential**; notes may be used in court

cards.q: What are the initial triage, privacy and consent requirements in alleged rape/sexual assault?
cards.a:
• **Triage** and examine in **privacy**
• **Police report**: for survivors **<18 years**, a police report **must be made urgently**
• **Written consent** required; **<18 years** consent from **parents, child protector or police officer**
• Managed by a **multidisciplinary team**
cards.m: Under 18: police urgently, consent by a guardian.

cards.q: What is done in acute (within 72 hours) management of sexual assault?
cards.a:
• **History and physical examination** (injuries documented)
• **Forensic evidence collection**: **clothing and debris**, **trace evidence**, **genital swabs**, **blood and urine samples**
• **Medical and preventive treatment** (EC, STI and tetanus prophylaxis, HIV PEP)

cards.q: What should a survivor of recent sexual assault be advised before forensic examination?
cards.a:
• Ideally **do not bathe, shower, douche, change clothes, urinate or brush teeth** before samples are taken
• Bring clothes in a **paper bag** (not plastic)
• Go directly to the **OSCC at the hospital emergency department**
• Medical care must **never be delayed** for evidence

cards.q: What emergency contraception is given after sexual assault?
cards.a:
• **Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose** (best within 72 hours)
• Or **copper IUD inserted within 5 days** (most effective)
• Do a **pregnancy test** first and again at follow-up

cards.q: What infection prophylaxis is given after sexual assault?
cards.a:
• **STI prophylaxis**: slide lists **doxycycline 100 mg BD + metronidazole** (written as 200 mg TDS for 2 weeks)
• Note: standard WHO regimens are **ceftriaxone** (gonorrhoea) + **azithromycin 1 g stat or doxycycline 100 mg BD 7 days** (chlamydia) + **metronidazole 2 g stat** (trichomonas)
• **Tetanus** prophylaxis for wounds
• **Hepatitis B vaccination** if non-immune; **HIV PEP**

cards.q: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after sexual assault: when and how?
cards.a:
• Start **as soon as possible**, ideally within hours, and **no later than 72 hours**
• **28-day** course of combination antiretrovirals
• **Baseline HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis** serology; repeat HIV at follow-up (about 6 weeks and 3 months)
• Beyond 72 h PEP is **not recommended** - offer testing and follow-up
cards.m: PEP: 72 hours to start, 28 days to finish.

cards.q: How is a 'cold' case (>72 hours) of sexual assault managed, and what follow-up is needed for all survivors?
cards.a:
• **Cold case (>72 h)**: forensic value is limited but still considered; focus on **clinical care** - **pregnancy test and STI management**
• Cu-IUD still possible up to 5 days
• **All survivors**: **social and psychological referral** (counselling, medical social worker) and **clinic follow-up**
• Watch for **PTSD, depression, suicidal ideation**

cards.q: A woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan within hours of a sexual assault. What is the next step?
cards.a:
• Ensure **immediate safety**, privacy and a **chaperone**; treat life-threatening injuries
• Give **first-line support** (LIVES) and explain options
• **Refer urgently to the OSCC** at the nearest hospital emergency department (forensic exam, PEP, police)
• Advise not to wash or change clothes; arrange **escort/transport**
• Document **her own words** and visible injuries
cards.m: KK stabilises and supports; OSCC investigates and treats.

cards.q: What are the three levels of crisis intervention in the One Stop Crisis Centre (OSCC)?
cards.a:
• **Level 1 - Initial management**: treatment and **police report**
• **Level 2 - Follow-up**: **O&G, paediatrics, social worker, psychiatry**
• **Level 3 - Rehabilitation**: social issues, **court** proceedings
cards.m: Treat → Follow → Rebuild.

cards.q: Which services and agencies make up the OSCC?
cards.a:
• Cases: **rape/sexual assault**, **child abuse and neglect**, **sodomy**, **domestic violence**
• Based in the hospital **emergency and trauma department**
• Team: **O&G, paediatrics, surgery, forensic, psychiatry**, **medical social services/counselling**
• Partners: **Social Welfare Department (JKM)**, **Royal Malaysian Police**, NGOs (e.g. **WCC**)

cards.q: Define home care.
cards.a:
• A broad approach providing **health services at the patient's home**
• Includes **home visits**, **phone follow-up/telehealth**, **counselling and education**
• **Complements** clinic-based care (does not replace it)
• Targets those with **limited access or special needs**

cards.q: What is the role of the health-care provider in home care?
cards.a:
• **Build rapport and trust**
• Use **assessment tools and checklists**
• Provide **education and counselling**
• **Identify red flags and arrange referral**
• **Document findings** and **plan follow-up**
cards.m: Rapport, Record, Refer.

cards.q: What are the benefits of home care?
cards.a:
• **Improves access** for vulnerable populations
• **Early detection and referral** of complications
• **Strengthens family involvement** and education
• Supports **mental health and emotional wellbeing**
• **Reduces preventable morbidity and mortality**

cards.q: What are the medical indications for children's home care?
cards.a:
• **Newborn at risk**: **low birth weight, preterm**
• **Sick newborn / recently discharged from NICU**
• **Congenital anomalies**
• **Developmental concerns**
• **Chronic illness** (epilepsy, asthma)

cards.q: What social indications justify children's home care?
cards.a:
• **Poor clinic follow-up**
• **Social risk**: **teenage mother**, poor family support, **suspected child neglect/abuse**
• Children of mothers with **special needs**: **maternal mental illness**, **substance abuse**

cards.q: What is assessed in a child during a home care visit?
cards.a:
• **Weight, height**, **temperature**
• Signs of **dehydration** and **respiratory distress**
• **Hygiene**, **nutrition** and **immunisation** status
• **Breastfeeding/feeding technique**
• **Medication adherence and technique** (inhalers, feeding tubes)
• **Developmental progress** and **home safety**

cards.q: What should caregivers be educated about during children's home care?
cards.a:
• **Danger signs** needing urgent care (poor feeding, lethargy, fast breathing, fits, jaundice spreading, fever in a young infant)
• **Hygiene**
• **Safe sleep**: baby **on the back**, firm flat surface, no pillows/soft toys, smoke-free room
cards.m: Back to sleep.

cards.q: Why are home visits particularly valuable for detecting child neglect or abuse?
cards.a:
• The worker sees the **real living environment**: hygiene, food, safety hazards, supervision
• Observes **caregiver-child interaction** and household stressors (substance use, violence)
• Concerns → **document** and refer to **SCAN team / OSCC** and **JKM** (social welfare)

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman, G2P1, attends Klinik Kesihatan for her first antenatal visit at 16 weeks by dates; she delayed because she was working abroad. The nurse records her history, BP, weight and urinalysis today.
By when should her first Routine Medical Examination (RME) by a doctor be completed?
o: At the first virtual consultation at 24-26 weeks
Within 4 weeks, once a repeat booking visit is held
During this visit or within 2 weeks after it
At 28 weeks, when visits become 2-weekly
Only after an 18-20 week anomaly scan is done
mcq.e: The booking visit should ideally be before 12 weeks, but a first visit done later is still the booking visit. The first RME must be done by a doctor during or within 2 weeks after the booking visit. Late booking is a reason to move faster, not to wait for later milestones.
w: Wrong - virtual consultations are for eligible mothers after booking and cannot replace the first doctor examination.
Wrong - there is no repeat booking visit; today's late first visit already counts as the booking visit.
Correct - the first RME is done by a doctor during or within 2 weeks of the booking visit, whatever the gestation.
Wrong - the change to 2-weekly visits at 28 weeks is unrelated to the timing of the first RME.
Wrong - the doctor review should not wait for a scan; dating and viability are part of the booking work-up.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old primigravida, white-coded, is seen at Klinik Kesihatan at 30 weeks. BP 112/70 mmHg, urine nil, SFH 30 cm. She prefers physical visits rather than virtual consultation.
When should her next routine physical antenatal visit be?
o: In 2 weeks, at 32 weeks
In 4 weeks, at 34 weeks
In 1 week, at 31 weeks
In 6 weeks, at 36 weeks
In 3 weeks, at 33 weeks
mcq.e: Routine visit frequency is monthly until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks to delivery. At 30 weeks she is in the 2-weekly band. High-risk mothers need more frequent visits than this.
w: Correct - between 28 and 36 weeks low-risk mothers are seen every 2 weeks.
Wrong - monthly (4-weekly) visits apply only until 28 weeks.
Wrong - weekly visits start from 36 weeks until delivery.
Wrong - a 6-week gap is longer than any routine interval in pregnancy.
Wrong - 3-weekly is not a routine interval in the MOH schedule.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman books at 10 weeks at Klinik Kesihatan. She was born in Malaysia, is well, has no cough, no travel history and no family history of thalassaemia. Ultrasound confirms a viable singleton pregnancy.
Which set of blood tests is routinely required for ALL booking mothers?
o: Hb, platelets, blood group, thalassaemia screen and malaria film
Hb, blood group, HIV, hepatitis B and TB interferon-gamma assay
Hb, platelets, blood group and Rhesus, HIV and hepatitis C
Hb, ferritin, blood group and Rhesus, syphilis and rubella IgM
Hb, platelets, blood group and Rhesus, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B
mcq.e: Every booking mother has Hb, platelets, blood group and Rhesus, plus infectious screening for syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B, because all three are vertically transmissible and preventable. Thalassaemia, malaria and TB screening are done only if indicated. Urinalysis for protein and sugar is also routine.
w: Wrong - thalassaemia and malaria screening are done only if indicated, and the infectious screen is missing.
Wrong - TB testing is only if indicated, and syphilis screening is omitted.
Wrong - hepatitis C is not part of the routine booking screen, and syphilis is missing.
Wrong - ferritin and rubella IgM are not routine booking tests, and HIV and hepatitis B are missing.
Correct - these are the universal booking bloods, with syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B as the infectious screen.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 books at 14 weeks at Klinik Kesihatan. Booking weight 43 kg, height 150 cm, BP 110/70 mmHg, Hb 11.5 g/dL, urine nil. Both previous deliveries were uncomplicated term vaginal births and she has no medical illness.
Which colour code and level of care is appropriate?
o: White - routine care by health or community nurses
